Calculus · Reference

Formula sheet

The formulas of the series in one place, from limits to vector calculus, each with the conditions under which it holds and the module that teaches it.

Every formula on this page was checked with the SymPy computer algebra system, as the worked examples of the modules are. Angles are in radians, ln⁡\lnln is the natural logarithm, and CCC is an arbitrary constant. The conditions beside a formula are part of it: outside them the formula can be false.

1

Algebra and trigonometry

The series assumes school algebra; the Optional algebra refresher of Mathematical Foundations revises it. Module 1 recalls the exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions.

L’Hôpital’s rule (Module 7, proved in Module 8). Let fff and ggg be differentiable on an open interval containing a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, except perhaps at a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, with g′(x)≠0g'(x) \ne 0g′(x)=0 there. Suppose fff and ggg both tend to 0, or both grow without bound in magnitude. If f′(x)g′(x)→L\dfrac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \to Lg′(x)f′(x)​→L as x→a,x \to a\mathclose{\text{,}}x→a, where LLL may be real or ±∞,\pm\infty\mathclose{\text{,}}±∞, then f(x)g(x)→L.\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} \to L\mathclose{\text{.}}g(x)f(x)​→L. For a one-sided limit use the corresponding side of a.a\mathclose{\text{.}}a. At ±∞\pm\infty±∞ the differentiability and nonzero-derivative conditions need only hold far enough along the relevant tail.

As everywhere in the series, the error of an estimate is the exact value minus the estimate, here f′(a)f'(a)f′(a) minus the difference. The two error estimates hold for small h>0h > 0h>0 when f′′f''f′′ (forward) or f′′′f'''f′′′ (central) is continuous near a.a\mathclose{\text{.}}a. In floating point, rounding adds an error of size about ε/h\varepsilon/hε/h for function values of order 1, where ε\varepsilonε is the scale of floating-point rounding. In double precision, steps of about 10−810^{-8}10−8 (forward) and 10−510^{-5}10−5 (central) can work well on that scale. The choice depends on the function values and derivatives.

Improper integrals

Module 12 teaches these. An improper integral converges when the limit that defines it exists and is finite:

∫a∞f(x) dx=lim⁡t→∞∫atf(x) dx,∫abf(x) dx=lim⁡t→b−∫atf(x) dx  if f is unbounded near b,\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^t f(x)\,dx, \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t\to b^-}\int_a^t f(x)\,dx \ \text{ if } f \text{ is unbounded near } b,∫a∞​f(x)dx=t→∞lim​∫at​f(x)dx,∫ab​f(x)dx=t→b−lim​∫at​f(x)dx  if f is unbounded near b,

provided each truncated integral is proper. Use the corresponding one-sided limit for a singularity at the left end. Split at any interior singularity and require convergence on both sides. Also, ∫−∞∞f(x) dx=∫−∞cf(x) dx+∫c∞f(x) dx\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^{c} f(x)\,dx + \int_{c}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=∫−∞c​f(x)dx+∫c∞​f(x)dx when both integrals on the right converge. (Both are needed: ∫−ttx dx=0\int_{-t}^{t} x\,dx = 0∫−tt​xdx=0 for every t,t\mathclose{\text{,}}t, yet ∫−∞∞x dx\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,dx∫−∞∞​xdx diverges.)

Lagrange multipliers. Suppose fff and the constraint functions have continuous first partials near a constrained extremum. Simple connectivity guarantees that the derivative test is sufficient. A field with a potential can also be conservative on a region with holes. For a case where the test fails to establish a potential, F=⟨−y,x⟩x2+y2\vb{F} = \dfrac{\langle -y, x\rangle}{x^2 + y^2}F=x2+y2⟨−y,x⟩​ has ∂P/∂y=∂Q/∂x\partial P/\partial y = \partial Q/\partial x∂P/∂y=∂Q/∂x away from the origin, yet its line integral once anticlockwise round the unit circle is 2π,2\pi\mathclose{\text{,}}2π, so it is not conservative on the punctured plane.

Green’s theorem ∮CP dx+Q dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y) dA{\displaystyle\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D \Big(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\Big)\,dA}∮C​Pdx+Qdy=∬D​(∂x∂Q​−∂y∂P​)dA C{C}C a piecewise smooth simple closed curve traced anticlockwise, bounding D;{D;}D; P,{P,}P, Q{Q}Q with continuous first partials on an open region containing D{D}D
Area from Green’s theorem A=12∮Cx dy−y dx{A = \dfrac12\displaystyle\oint_C x\,dy - y\,dx}A=21​∮C​xdy−ydx the same C{C}C and D{D}D
Stokes’ theorem ∮CF⋅dr=∬Scurl⁡F⋅dS{\displaystyle\oint_C \vb{F}\cdot d\vb{r} = \iint_S \operatorname{curl}\vb{F}\cdot d\vb{S}}∮C​F⋅dr=∬S​curlF⋅dS S{S}S oriented and piecewise smooth, with piecewise smooth simple closed boundary C{C}C oriented by S.{S}\mathclose{\text{.}}S. The field has continuous first partials on a neighbourhood of S{S}S
Divergence theorem ∬SF⋅dS=∭Ediv⁡F dV{\displaystyle\iint_S \vb{F}\cdot d\vb{S} = \iiint_E \operatorname{div}\vb{F}\,dV}∬S​F⋅dS=∭E​divFdV S{S}S is the outward-oriented, piecewise smooth boundary of a bounded solid E.{E}\mathclose{\text{.}}E. The field has continuous first partials on a neighbourhood of E{E}E

All five fundamental theorems (of calculus, for line integrals, Green’s, Stokes’ and the divergence theorem) have the same shape: integrating a derivative over a region gives the corresponding boundary expression (the two ends of an interval or a curve, the edge of a surface, the surface of a solid).

9

SymPy commands

The commands the series uses, written as in its “Compute it” boxes, after import sympy as sp. The module column points to explanations and examples.

Command What it does Module
sp.symbols('x n') creates symbols: x, n = sp.symbols('x n'); positive=True adds an assumption 1, 6
f.subs(x, 2) substitutes 2{2}2 for x{x}x in f 1
sp.expand(f) expands products and powers 1
sp.factor(f) factorises 1
sp.simplify(f) simplifies 1
sp.N(f, 10) a numerical approximation to f at 10 significant digits of precision 1
sp.lambdify(x, f) turns f into a callable for numerical evaluation 1
sp.log(x) ln⁡x,{\ln x,}lnx, as is math.log(x); sp.log(x, 10) is log⁡10x{\log_{10} x}log10​x 1
sp.limit(f, x, a, '+-') the limit as x→a;{x \to a;}x→a; without '+-' SymPy gives the limit from the right ('+', its default); '-' gives the limit from the left 2
sp.oo ∞,{\infty,}∞, as in sp.limit(f, x, sp.oo) 2, 3
sp.diff(f, x) the derivative; sp.diff(f, x, 2) is the second derivative 4
sp.solve(f, x) tries to solve f=0{f=0}f=0 for x. It returns a list when it solves a single equation for one symbol 8
sp.summation(a, (n, 1, N)) the sum ∑n=1Na;{\sum_{n=1}^{N} a;}∑n=1N​a; N{N}N may be sp.oo 9, 14
sp.integrate(f, x) tries to find an antiderivative, without + C{+\,C}+C 10
sp.integrate(f, (x, a, b)) tries to evaluate the definite integral ∫abf dx{\int_a^b f\,dx}∫ab​fdx 10
sp.dsolve(eq, y(x)) tries to solve a differential equation; first y = sp.Function('y') 13
sp.series(f, x, a, n) expands near a{a}a to order n,{n}\mathclose{\text{,}}n, usually with an O((x−a)n){O\big((x-a)^n\big)}O((x−a)n) remainder. A Taylor expansion is the case with ordinary nonnegative integer powers 15
Compute itEleven commands in one session
Python
import sympy as sp
x, n = sp.symbols('x n')
y = sp.Function('y')
f = x**2 * sp.exp(x)
print("diff:     ", sp.diff(f, x))
print("integrate:", sp.integrate(f, x))
print("definite: ", sp.integrate(f, (x, 0, 1)))
print("limit:    ", sp.limit(sp.sin(x)/x, x, 0, '+-'))
print("series:   ", sp.series(sp.cos(x), x, 0, 6))
print("solve:    ", sp.solve(x**2 - 5*x + 6, x))
print("summation:", sp.summation(1/n**2, (n, 1, sp.oo)))
print("dsolve:   ", sp.dsolve(y(x).diff(x) - 2*y(x), y(x)))
print("N:        ", sp.N(sp.pi, 10))
print("simplify: ", sp.simplify(sp.sin(x)**2 + sp.cos(x)**2))
print("lambdify: ", sp.lambdify(x, f)(1.0))
Output
diff:      x**2*exp(x) + 2*x*exp(x)
integrate: (x**2 - 2*x + 2)*exp(x)
definite:  -2 + E
limit:     1
series:    1 - x**2/2 + x**4/24 + O(x**6)
solve:     [2, 3]
summation: pi**2/6
dsolve:    Eq(y(x), C1*exp(2*x))
N:         3.141592654
simplify:  1
lambdify:  2.718281828459045

SymPy writes E for eee and exp(x) for ex,e^x\mathclose{\text{,}}ex, so the definite integral is e−2.e - 2\mathclose{\text{.}}e−2. The antiderivative (x2−2x+2)ex(x^2 - 2x + 2)e^x(x2−2x+2)ex comes without + C,+\,C\mathclose{\text{,}}+C, while dsolve names its arbitrary constant C1. The series of cos⁡x\cos xcosx stops before x6x^6x6 and says so with O(x**6). sp.N gives π\piπ to 10 significant digits, and the function made by sp.lambdify returns an ordinary floating-point number: e1≈2.718281828459045.e^1 \approx 2.718281828459045\mathclose{\text{.}}e1≈2.718281828459045.
